idiom_name: copy-and-assign helpers, optionally a per-type getter/setter struct
implementation_notes: C has no closures, no generics and no immutability: the lens structure degrades to per-field helpers that copy the whole struct by value and reassign one member - `Person person_with_city(Person p, const char *city) { Person out = p; out.city = city; return out; }` - because struct assignment copies every member (cppreference, Assignment operators). A real lens is still writable by hand as a struct of function pointers specialised per type (`const char *(*get)(const Person *); Person (*set)(Person, const char *);`), but composing two of them needs a `void *` context plus casts, so the classic composable form is justified only where code generation or macros emit one lens per field and the same update path is reused at many call sites; elsewhere the explicit copy helper is shorter and type-safe.
pitfalls: The struct copy is shallow: two Person values share the buffers their `char *` members point at, so "immutable" values must own their memory or explicitly accept aliasing.
Copying a large struct on every update costs stack traffic, and without closures every composed path has to be unrolled by hand (or carry a `void *` context that discards type safety).
There is no const-enforcement of the discipline: `const Person *` stops this function from writing, but nothing stops another function from mutating the original struct in place.
